The Bone-gatherers was the title of a satyr play by Aeschylus (fr. 177-179).

Arcadius p. 85, 25 noted the accent ὀστολόγος [bone-gatherer]. But the bones are to be understood as those of the dead, about which the grammarian in Bekker p. 286, 23 noted the verb ὀστολογῆσαι [to gather bones].
Bone-gatherers: in Epilycus. And a drama of Aeschylus, Bone-gatherers
of shells: those of the egg
of shells: “unfledged, tiny, just naked from the shells.” Instead of eggs. But some say from the coverings

unless he wrote ὠστρακωμένη [shattered], which participle Lycophron used at v. 88.
and struck upon my head, the chamber pot was wrecked, shattered
In the codex is κ᾿ ὄστρεα [and oysters]. Correctly Athenaeus p. 92e: “The ancients said ὄστρεια [oysters] only thus.”
The ancients said oysters only thus
Hippocrates used this adjective at p. 73, 120, 169 and 209, and likewise the verb ὀσφυαλγέω [to suffer from hip pain] and the noun ὀσφυαλγία [hip pain].
from a hip-pained and pain-wracked, wretched old man
